title: Ron &Amp; Tammy: Part Two

jokes.text: The overdue library book is titled 'It's Not the Size of the Boat: Embracing Life with a Micro-Penis.'
jokes.setup: A bureaucrat from the controller's office arrives to awkwardly inform Ron about an outstanding debt from an overdue library book.
jokes.punchline: The book title — 'It's Not the Size of the Boat: Embracing Life with a Micro-Penis' — is an absurd and humiliating title planted by Tammy to embarrass Ron publicly.
jokes.explanation: A near-perfect cold open joke. The bureaucratic framing (controller's office, official letter, awkward delivery) sets up the punchline beautifully. The book title is maximally specific and humiliating — it attacks Ron's core identity as a hyper-masculine man while being delivered via the most boring possible channel (a collection agency letter). Character integration is exceptional: only Tammy would weaponize library bureaucracy against Ron Swanson specifically. The slow build of 'It's Not the Size of the Boat' before the mic-drop second half is textbook structure.

dialogue.speaker: Jack Cooper
dialogue.line: Mr. Swanson, you have an overdue book from the library.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: That's impossible. I don't read.

dialogue.speaker: Jack Cooper
dialogue.line: According to our records, you checked out 'The Joy of Feelings: A Sensitive Man's Guide to Emotional Expression.'

jokes.text: Ron's talking head: 'My ex-wife Tammy likes to check in every so often and make sure I'm doing okay. And if I am, she tries to [bleep] everything up.'
jokes.setup: Ron calmly explains Tammy's visiting pattern as if describing a routine wellness check.
jokes.punchline: The bleeping of the verb makes it funnier than any specific word; the calm, clinical tone describing something monstrous is perfectly Ron.
jokes.explanation: The joke earns its score through Ron's deadpan delivery of something genuinely dark. The two-beat structure — 'she checks if I'm okay / and if I am, she destroys it' — is tight and efficient. The bleep amplifies the absurdity by letting the audience's imagination fill in the worst. High character integration: the flat, stoic delivery is quintessential Ron. Justifies the 8+ because the construction is genuinely skilled and the character voice is irreplaceable.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: She's been very supportive. Brings me soup when I'm sick, remembers my birthday, asks about my day.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: It's almost like she still cares about me.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Then I realized — she's gathering intelligence. Every piece of information is ammunition for future sabotage.

jokes.text: Leslie pre-dials 911 and tells Ron: 'If she binds your hands and you can't reach your phone, just try to chew yourself free.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is trying to help Ron prepare for an encounter with Tammy by pre-dialing 911.
jokes.punchline: 'If she binds your hands and you can't reach your phone, just try to chew yourself free' — delivered as earnest, practical advice.
jokes.explanation: Excellent joke. The premise of pre-dialing 911 as a safety measure is already funny, but escalating to 'chew yourself free' elevates it into the genuinely dark absurdist territory this show excels at. Fully character-integrated: Leslie's hyper-competent, over-prepared nature delivers something horrifying as if it were a standard operating procedure. Highly quotable. Justifies 8+ because it combines character voice, dark escalation, and a genuinely surprising specific image ('chew yourself free') that you don't see coming.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, when you meet with Tammy, you need to be careful. Bring a friend, stay in public, keep your phone charged.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Leslie, it's just coffee.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Just coffee? Ron, this is Tammy we're talking about. You need to have an exit strategy. Leave your car running. Keep a go-bag in your trunk with cash, fake passports, and a change of clothes.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: That seems excessive.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: And if she tries to take you across state lines, you fight back. Bite if you have to. Aim for the eyes and the throat. And if she somehow manages to throw you in the back of a van, you kick out the tail lights so law enforcement can track you.

jokes.text: 'Whale tale. Whale tale. She's flashing a whale tale. Abort. Abort.'
jokes.setup: Ron and Leslie approach the library; Tammy is bent over, visible thong showing.
jokes.punchline: Ron whisper-commands 'Whale tale. Abort. Abort.' — tactical military language applied to a whale tail sighting — before Tammy straightens up and greets them.
jokes.explanation: The military tactical language ('abort, abort') applied to a whale tail is perfectly Ron — he treats even mundane danger with hyper-serious operational discipline. The repetition and urgency amplify the comedy. Strong character integration and economy.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ron, I've got visual on a Code Yellow. I repeat, Code Yellow.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: What is it?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Visible panty line. Two o'clock.

jokes.text: Tammy: 'I was just checking myself for scoliosis.' Beat. 'Straight as an arrow. Just like somebody else I know.'
jokes.setup: Ron catches Tammy bent over provocatively; she offers the cover story of checking herself for scoliosis.
jokes.punchline: 'Straight as an arrow. Just like somebody else I know' — a shameless, double-entendre flirtation delivered with total confidence.
jokes.explanation: Tammy's brazenness is the joke here — the obvious lie delivered as fact, followed by a shameless double entendre. The character voice is strong. The 'straight as an arrow' pivot is clean and quick. Not quite exceptional but well above average.

dialogue.speaker: Tammy
dialogue.line: I'm very progressive about these things. Women should be comfortable examining their own bodies.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: That's... actually a reasonable position.

dialogue.speaker: Tammy
dialogue.line: I know. And you should try it too.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm perfectly straight.

dialogue.speaker: Tammy
dialogue.line: That's the problem.

jokes.text: Ron's talking head: 'I admit there was a time when that sort of behavior would've driven me wild. But I am in a healthy relationship now, Tammy.'
jokes.setup: Ron is clearly flustered by Tammy's seductive behavior
jokes.punchline: The talking head cuts to Ron delivering this with unconvincing stoicism directly addressing Tammy as if she can hear him — breaking the confessional format weirdly and showing he's already rattled
jokes.explanation: A competent talking-head joke that reveals character — Ron's stoic denial is undercut by the fact that he's directly addressing Tammy, showing he's already thinking about her. Not particularly quotable or original but functionally good character work.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: That's so hot.

jokes.text: Tammy responds to Ron calling his new girlfriend 'a lovely, intelligent, self-possessed pediatric surgeon named Wendy' with: 'Sounds like a real whore.'
jokes.setup: Ron describes his new girlfriend in flattering, dignified terms to demonstrate he's moved on.
jokes.punchline: Tammy immediately and confidently responds 'Sounds like a real whore' — the perfect non-sequitur character-revealing line.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. In five words, 'Sounds like a real whore' does enormous character work: it reveals Tammy's jealousy, her refusal to engage with reality, and her weaponized vulgarity — all while being maximally economical. The setup is a long dignified list of virtues, making the sheer wrongness of the response funnier. Highly quotable. Justifies 8+ because it's an almost perfectly crafted character line with flawless economy and maximum impact.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: She's intelligent, independent, and has a wonderful sense of humor.

dialogue.speaker: Tammy
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, she sounds like a real piece of work. Probably a nightmare in bed.

jokes.text: Leslie's awkward talking head: 'Good day, Leslie. Good... good day.'
jokes.setup: Ron dismisses Tammy with a formal 'Good day' and exits; Leslie is left standing awkwardly.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's confessional re-enacts her own useless response — 'Good... good day' — illustrating her social freeze.
jokes.explanation: The self-mocking talking head is a mockumentary staple done well here. Leslie re-enacting her own inadequate response is charming and character-consistent. Modest but functional.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm going to say goodbye now.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Goodbye.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Goodbye.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Goodbye.

jokes.text: Ben suggests salads for the cops; Leslie says 'Wow, don't be such a Jerry, Ben.' Tom adds: 'Yeah, Ben, these guys are cops, not ballerinas.'
jokes.setup: Ben makes a sensible suggestion to include healthy options for the police party.
jokes.punchline: Two successive put-downs comparing him to Jerry (the office punching bag) and then calling cops 'not ballerinas.'
jokes.explanation: 'Don't be such a Jerry' is an efficient running gag callback using Jerry's name as a generic insult. 'Cops, not ballerinas' is a decent punchy follow. Together they work as a tag-team put-down. Competent but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: What about some healthy options for the police officers? Maybe some grilled chicken, steamed vegetables?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ben, don't be such a Jerry.

jokes.text: 'Calzones are like pizzas but they're harder to eat. They're dumb and so was that idea.'
jokes.setup: Someone suggests calzones as an alternative to pizza.
jokes.punchline: Leslie demolishes the idea with unusual conviction: 'They're dumb and so was that idea.'
jokes.explanation: The joke works on two levels: the objectively correct observation that calzones ARE pizza that's harder to eat, and Leslie's disproportionate hostility toward them. The 'they're dumb and so was that idea' tag is efficient and funny. Also seeds the running calzone gag that pays off later. Strong economy.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Hey, you know what? Salad is what food eats.

jokes.text: Ron announces he's going for 'a mid-morning pre-lunch' before returning 'in time for lunch.'
jokes.setup: Ron excuses himself from the party planning meeting.
jokes.punchline: 'A mid-morning pre-lunch... but I will be back in time for lunch' — Ron's commitment to meal times is so absolute he has invented a new meal category.
jokes.explanation: Pure Ron Swanson character comedy. The invention of 'mid-morning pre-lunch' as a distinct meal is funny because it's so earnest and so specifically him. The callback of 'but I will be back in time for lunch' makes clear this is a non-negotiable schedule. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: We should get calzones! They're amazing.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Calzones are just pizza that's afraid to be itself. They're cowards. And you suggesting them makes you a coward too.

jokes.text: Tom's talking head about imagining Ron with a cape while 'plowing' his ex-wife, and Ben accidentally making it worse.
jokes.setup: Tom is disturbed that Ron is dating his ex-wife Wendy. He describes only being able to think of 'Captain Mustache plowing my ex-wife.'
jokes.punchline: Ben, trying to help, suggests imagining Ron in a cape — which accidentally makes it funnier/worse. Tom: 'Now, I'm imagining a cape.'
jokes.explanation: A beautifully constructed two-beat cringe joke. Tom's coining 'Captain Mustache' is already great, but Ben's well-meaning suggestion backfiring — forcing Tom (and the audience) to now involuntarily visualize Ron in a cape — is the escalation that makes it. 'Now, I'm imagining a cape' as the final line is perfectly resigned. High structure score because the callback of the suggestion undoing itself is elegant.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ron and Tammy got back together? That's impossible. Ron hates Tammy more than he hates the government, and he hates the government.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Well, they do have a lot in common.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Yeah, like what? Evil?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I was thinking more like they're both really into woodworking and breakfast meats.

jokes.text: April trolls Chris's post-it request: 'You want five million orange post-its.' Chris: 'That's hilarious.'
jokes.setup: Chris meticulously specifies which post-it colors he wants ('Do not buy orange. I have plenty of orange.').
jokes.punchline: April summarizes: 'You want five million orange post-its.' Chris doesn't notice the sarcasm and calls it 'hilarious.'
jokes.explanation: Works as a character contrast joke: April's deadpan passive aggression vs. Chris's bottomless positivity that can't register sarcasm. Chris calling it 'hilarious' adds a layer — he's so positive that even insults bounce off him. Solid character integration for both.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I heard you don't want orange post-its.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: So I got you orange post-its.

jokes.text: Chris gives April a post-it that says 'great job' and enthusiastically tells her 'Great job!'
jokes.setup: Chris has a post-it for April; the implication is it's an important message.
jokes.punchline: The post-it just says 'great job' — Chris's absurd positivity manifesting as a physical artifact, which he then reads aloud as if it adds meaning.
jokes.explanation: A gentle Chris character joke. His relentless positivity is so extreme that he hands out literal written affirmations. Functional, character-consistent, but not surprising — Chris's optimism is well-established by this point in the series.

dialogue.speaker: Wendy
dialogue.line: My family needs me in Canada. It's not complicated. They're my responsibility, and I'm going to be there for them.

jokes.text: Chris's assistant talking head: explains parents are getting old and he's an only child, then trails off — 'I just feel like the right thing to do is to move back home. I'm sorry to see you go. I've really come to think of you as...'
jokes.setup: Chris is mid-confessional, explaining his assistant's departure.
jokes.punchline: A long pause, then '...a companion' — delivered with genuine emotion but the word choice is so clinical and distant that it's absurd.
jokes.explanation: The pause before 'a companion' is the joke — Chris's emotional depth fails him at the crucial moment and he lands on the most impersonal possible word. Reveals his character flaw (inability to be truly intimate despite performing warmth) economically.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Wendy and I have what I'd call a professional relationship. We respect each other's work ethic and we share similar values about government efficiency.

dialogue.speaker: Wendy
dialogue.line: Ron, I've been thinking... what if we moved to Canada together?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: No.

jokes.text: Chris asks his departing assistant, 'Hey, I don't suppose you'd want to move to Canada?' Long pause. 'No, I don't suppose I would.'
jokes.setup: Chris makes a last-ditch offer to keep his assistant.
jokes.punchline: The assistant calmly, definitively declines — the flatness of 'No, I don't suppose I would' matching the absurdity of being asked to immigrate for a temp job.
jokes.explanation: A quiet, well-timed joke. The mirrored phrasing ('I don't suppose' / 'No, I don't suppose I would') is elegant. Functional cringe comedy of watching someone fail to retain an employee. Modest score because it's a low-key moment.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I taught Wendy to whittle. She's a natural.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Look at this. She made it in just three hours.

jokes.text: Leslie outlines the exact strategy: 'Post pizza, pre ice cream, between his third and fourth beer. He'll be full but not stuffed, tipsy but not drunk. Should be around 9:00.'
jokes.setup: Ben asks when they should ask the chief the big favor.
jokes.punchline: Leslie has a hyper-specific psychological manipulation schedule worked out to the beer number and fullness level.
jokes.explanation: Quintessential Leslie Knope comedy: she has a rigorously detailed plan for everything, even social manipulation at a party. 'Full but not stuffed, tipsy but not drunk' is a perfectly balanced parallel construction. High character integration — only Leslie would approach favor-asking as a tactical science.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, you need to get back out there. You can't let one bad relationship define you.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Leslie, I appreciate the sentiment, but I'm a man. That advice is for women.

jokes.text: Ron, just broken up with Wendy, tells Leslie: 'I just taught her how to whittle. She made me this tiny sharpened stick.'
jokes.setup: Leslie expresses sympathy over Ron's breakup.
jokes.punchline: Ron's only expressed regret is that he had just taught Wendy to whittle; he holds up the tiny sharpened stick as if it were the real loss.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. Ron's stoicism means he can't or won't express emotional pain — so the closest he comes is lamenting the practical loss of a newly trained whittling partner, evidenced by 'this tiny sharpened stick.' The specificity of 'tiny sharpened stick' is perfect: it's the saddest, most useless object imaginable as a romantic memento. Could ONLY be Ron Swanson. Justifies 8+ because of extraordinary character integration, economy, and the quietly devastating emotional subtext.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: You know, I've been thinking about calzones lately.

dialogue.speaker: Chief
dialogue.line: No.

jokes.text: Leslie tells a freshly dumped Ron: 'Look, I'm gonna tell you what I tell all my girlfriends when they get dumped. Men are dogs.' Ron: 'That does not apply to this situation at all. But thank you.'
jokes.setup: Leslie tries to comfort Ron with her go-to breakup advice.
jokes.punchline: Ron politely acknowledges the advice is completely inapplicable while thanking her anyway — his stoic dignity intact.
jokes.explanation: Two-character joke that works for both: Leslie's rote advice delivered by pure reflex, and Ron's gentlemanly correction. The rhythm of 'That does not apply to this situation at all. But thank you.' is perfectly calibrated — the pause before 'but thank you' is doing a lot of work.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Look, Tammy Two is just a woman. She's not a demon, she's not a witch, she's not a supernatural being of pure evil.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: She's just a regular person who happens to be awful, and mean, and cruel, and sadistic, and possibly a vampire.

jokes.text: Chris orders a beer with extraordinary specificity: 'I would like a local beer. I'd like it in a bottle. I'd like the bottle to be cold.' Then orders wine: 'I would like it to be chardonnay. And I would like that with one ice cube.'
jokes.setup: Chris and Ann are at the bar at the police party.
jokes.punchline: The extreme specificity of 'one ice cube' after the already-fussy beer order is the escalating punchline — he's treating the bartender like a personal barista.
jokes.explanation: The joke is Chris's control-freak wellness persona extending to social drinking. 'One ice cube' is the escalating final beat. Functional character comedy that reinforces his established traits.

dialogue.speaker: Tammy II
dialogue.line: When a man and woman love each other very much, the man puts his penis inside the woman's vagina.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: It's Tom.

dialogue.speaker: Tammy II
dialogue.line: I know who you are.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: No, I mean... it's just Tom. Not 'a man.' Tom.

jokes.text: Chief Trumple tells Ben 'I just said it was good pizza' when Ben calls it 'dynamite' — then immediately says 'You know what I like? Calzones.'
jokes.setup: Leslie and Ben are trying to warm up the chief. Ben enthusiastically oversells the pizza as 'dynamite.'
jokes.punchline: The chief corrects him ('I just said it was good pizza'), then pivots to the one food Leslie has already declared war on: calzones.
jokes.explanation: Excellent structural callback. The chief preferring calzones after Leslie's passionate anti-calzone speech is a great plant-and-payoff. Ben's over-eager 'dynamite' being corrected flat is also a nice character beat. The double payload (Ben's social failure + calzone callback) makes this punchy.

dialogue.speaker: Police Officer
dialogue.line: On the evening of April 15th, officers responded to a disturbance at the residence of one Ronald Duffy Swanson. Upon arrival, we discovered the subject engaged in a heated altercation with an individual identified as Tammy Preston.

dialogue.speaker: Police Officer
dialogue.line: The subject, Mr. Swanson, was found to be a real piece of work. A real piece of work. In all my years on the force, I have never encountered a real piece of work quite like him.

jokes.text: Ben's horrified talking head: 'What the hell is wrong with this guy?' after the calzone reveal.
jokes.setup: The chief announces he likes calzones right after Leslie's rant.
jokes.punchline: Ben's camera look — pure bewildered outrage — is the audience surrogate reaction.
jokes.explanation: A solid reaction beat that extends the calzone running gag. Ben's exasperation is funny but relatively standard talking-head comedy. The joke is mostly in the callback rather than any craft in the delivery.

dialogue.speaker: Tammy
dialogue.line: We got matching tattoos.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Where?

dialogue.speaker: Tammy
dialogue.line: On our butts.

jokes.text: Tom introduces Tammy as his date and says: 'Is seeing your ex-wife on my arm making you uncomfortable? Gee, I can't imagine why. Or can I?'
jokes.setup: Tom has brought Tammy to the police party specifically to spite Ron.
jokes.punchline: 'Gee, I can't imagine why. Or can I?' — cartoonishly obvious villain dialogue delivered by Tom as if he's won something.
jokes.explanation: Tom's petty villainy is funny because he's so transparently bad at it. The 'Gee, I can't imagine why. Or can I?' is clichéd on purpose — it makes Tom look like an amateur schemer. Functional but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Hi, this is April Ludgate calling on behalf of Chris Traeger from the Parks Department. Yes, I'll hold.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Hi, thanks for waiting. Chris wanted me to reach out because he values your input and respects your opinion. Also, Ann doesn't care what you think, so it's just me.

jokes.text: Leslie's talking head describing Tammy: 'A manipulative, psychotic, library-book-pedaling, sex-crazed she-demon.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is explaining why Tammy is dangerous.
jokes.punchline: The list escalates from reasonable descriptors to 'library-book-pedaling, sex-crazed she-demon' — the specificity of 'library-book-pedaling' as a character flaw is absurdly funny.
jokes.explanation: The list builds nicely — 'manipulative, psychotic' are standard, but 'library-book-pedaling' is hyper-specific to the world of the show (Leslie's institutional hatred of libraries) and 'sex-crazed she-demon' lands as a comedic crescendo. Highly quotable phrase with strong character specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, part of your mustache is missing.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I know.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: It'll grow back.

jokes.text: Tammy introduces herself as having 'tasted' Tom — 'I was just tasting my new boyfriend, Glenn.' Tom corrects her: 'Tom.'
jokes.setup: Tammy has been making out with Tom and addresses the group.
jokes.punchline: She calls Tom 'Glenn,' demonstrating she doesn't even know his name — and 'tasting' as a euphemism is grotesque and funny.
jokes.explanation: The word 'tasting' is doing heavy lifting — it's both accurate and disturbing. Not knowing Tom's name diminishes him further while establishing Tammy as someone who uses people instrumentally. Strong Tammy character work.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, we're here because we care about you. You're addicted to relationships.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: That's ridiculous.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You've been through three marriages. You're chasing that first high, that initial rush of commitment. You need an intervention.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I don't have a problem.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, you're a relationship junkie. And like all junkies, you need to hit rock bottom before you can recover.

jokes.text: Ron tells Tom: 'You don't know what you're mixed up in, son. This isn't about you. It's about me.'
jokes.setup: Tom thinks he's the one using Tammy to make Ron jealous.
jokes.punchline: Ron, with complete paternal authority, tells Tom he is merely a pawn in a larger game — 'This isn't about you. It's about me.'
jokes.explanation: 'Son' alone is a great character beat — Ron speaks to Tom with exactly the kind of weary paternal condescension you'd expect. The structure of warning someone they're in over their head while making it entirely about himself is funny and earned.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ron, you look like a bald eagle had a baby with a steak.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: A bald, beautiful, steak eagle.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: You're majestic.

jokes.text: Four police officers simultaneously describe the domestic disturbance using overlapping cop jargon: 'White male, 40, 45.' 'Caucasian male.' 'Stocky build.' 'Approximately 5'10".' ...'Real piece of work.' 'Real piece of work.' 'Real piece of work.' 'Real piece of work.'
jokes.setup: Four cops are simultaneously filing verbal reports on Ron and Tammy's argument.
jokes.punchline: The overlapping bureaucratic police jargon applied to a soap-opera domestic scene, culminating in all four cops independently arriving at the same non-jargon conclusion: 'Real piece of work.'
jokes.explanation: Brilliant structural joke. The comedy escalates through layered cop-speak being applied absurdly to an interpersonal dispute, then all four independent threads converge on the same colloquial phrase: 'Real piece of work.' — said four times in a row. The convergence is the punchline. The repetition amplifies rather than dilutes because each 'real piece of work' is a separate cop arriving at the same frustrated conclusion independently. Justifies 8+ for structural cleverness and the satisfying convergence punchline.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ron is like my brother. My actual brother, not like a metaphorical brother thing. My real brother who shares my parents.

jokes.text: Cut to Ron and Tammy hours later. Ron is in a kimono with cornrows. Leslie slaps him: 'Snap out of it!'
jokes.setup: Ron announced he and Tammy were going to 'get coffee and talk things out' and 'bury the hatchet.'
jokes.punchline: The cut reveals Ron transformed — kimono, cornrows — as evidence of what actually happened in the intervening hours.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's standout visual gags. Ron Swanson — the most rigidly stoic, masculine, anti-ostentation character on television — revealed in a kimono with cornrows is maximum comedic violation of character. The cut structure (before: 'We're just going to talk' / after: utter debasement) is perfect. The visual alone earns a 9+ because it's so specifically wrong for Ron. Justifies 8+ definitively.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Ron, buddy, I'm gonna give you some real talk. You need to open up more, share your feelings, let people in. But also, you gotta learn to be alone, you know? Really embrace solitude. And you should definitely get married, but also never get married because it's a trap. Oh, and you need to make more friends, but also stop wasting time on people who don't matter. Just be yourself, but also try to be better. It's all about balance, man.

jokes.text: Leslie slaps Ron and yells 'Snap out of it!' Ron calmly says 'Leslie.' Then: 'Congratulate us. Ron's got one just like it on his penis.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is trying to bring Ron to his senses after his Tammy-induced transformation.
jokes.punchline: Tammy casually reveals matching tattoos — including one 'on his penis' — as if this is a perfectly normal announcement.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional joke. 'Ron's got one just like it on his penis' delivered with Tammy's casual possessive pride is perfectly constructed. The economy is flawless — five words deliver maximum information (they've had sex, they got tattoos, one is on his penis) with maximum comedic payload. It's both character-specific (Tammy's shamelessness) and a devastating update on Ron's condition. Highly quotable. Justifies 8+ easily.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: If you're watching this, it means I've made a terrible mistake. I've gotten involved with a woman again.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: A man is like a wolf. And a woman is like a beautiful forest. And the wolf wants to stay in the forest forever, but the forest keeps burning down, over and over again.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: And the wolf just wants to run free through the trees, but he can't, because his paws keep getting burned.

jokes.text: Flashback/explanation montage of what happened at the courthouse: Ron wins at something, yells 'Rock and roll! Yeah, baby!'; then 'You may now kiss the bride.'
jokes.setup: Leslie asks what happened. The audience gets the montage answer.
jokes.punchline: They got married at the courthouse — Ron Swanson, arch-conservative libertarian, is now re-married to his demon ex-wife within a few hours.
jokes.explanation: The reveal that Ron has re-married Tammy in the span of an evening is a strong structural payoff. 'Rock and roll! Yeah, baby!' as an out-of-character exclamation from Ron signals how thoroughly Tammy has unmanned him. The wedding as the culminating escalation of 'coffee' → tattoos → marriage is well-paced.

dialogue.speaker: Past Ron
dialogue.line: You have two choices: either you break up with her, or you undergo a series of extreme medical procedures.

dialogue.speaker: Past Ron
dialogue.line: We're talking full body replacement surgery, organ transplants, possibly a complete consciousness transfer into a new body.

dialogue.speaker: Past Ron
dialogue.line: Those are your only two options.

jokes.text: April calls Ann on Chris's behalf but tells her Chris can't make lunch, then adds: 'I knew you wouldn't care. Good-bye.'
jokes.setup: Chris asks April to call Ann and apologize for missing lunch.
jokes.punchline: April delivers the message, then pre-empts any response by saying 'I knew you wouldn't care. Good-bye.' and hanging up.
jokes.explanation: Peak April Ludgate — she completes the task with maximum passive aggression, preemptively dismissing Ann's reaction and hanging up before she can respond. 'I knew you wouldn't care. Good-bye.' is a perfect encapsulation of April's character: contemptuous, efficient, and weirdly honest. High economy and character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Tammy and I are getting married and leaving the department.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Tammy's been on fertility treatments for three years. Her uterus is like a frozen burrito—you have to keep rotating it or it'll cook unevenly.

jokes.text: Chief: 'I don't want him within 500 feet of the library.' Leslie: 'That's good advice for all of us. Nothing but trouble there.'
jokes.setup: The chief issues a restraining order-style directive about the library.
jokes.punchline: Leslie earnestly agrees — 'good advice for all of us' — treating the library as a universal hazard, consistent with the show's running joke about Leslie's institutional rivalry with libraries.
jokes.explanation: The Leslie-hates-libraries running joke is well-deployed here. Her heartfelt agreement that libraries are dangerous for everyone is consistent and funny — the institutional rivalry treated as common wisdom.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Leslie and I are preparing for our honeymoon. I've made a list of supplies we'll need.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Forty-seven bottles of coconut oil, industrial-sized box of condoms, noise-canceling headphones, and a 'Do Not Disturb' sign the size of a window.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm not taking any chances. We have very important work to do.

jokes.text: Ron in the car: 'Take me back to Tammy.' Leslie: 'For the millionth time, no.' Ron: 'This is our song.' Leslie: 'Your song is Dancing on the Ceiling by Lionel Richie?'
jokes.setup: Ron is being driven away from Tammy and is completely in her thrall.
jokes.punchline: Ron claiming a Lionel Richie song as 'their song' — antithetical to everything Ron Swanson represents — is the joke.
jokes.explanation: The specific choice of 'Dancing on the Ceiling' — a cheesy, maximally anti-Ron pop song — is perfect. It shows how completely Tammy has corrupted his taste alongside everything else. Leslie's incredulous delivery of the song title makes the joke land.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Dear citizen, this is an emergency letter from Ron Swanson.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: If you are reading this, I am probably dead or in a very bad mood, which is basically the same thing.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Signed, Bert Macklin, FBI.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'Oh, wow, look at that. You shaved off part of your mustache.' Ron: 'I didn't shave it off. It rubbed off... from friction.'
jokes.setup: Leslie notices Ron's mustache is partially missing.
jokes.punchline: 'It rubbed off... from friction' — a devastatingly matter-of-fact explanation of vigorous sexual activity delivered with total stoicism.
jokes.explanation: An exceptional joke. The setup (visual observation about a missing mustache patch) is innocent. The punchline ('rubbed off from friction') is maximally economical and horrifyingly clear without being explicit. The pause before 'from friction' — indicated by the ellipsis — is doing structural work: it lets Leslie (and the audience) hang for a beat before the awful truth arrives. Could only be Ron's mustache. The specificity of mustache-friction-as-evidence-of-sex is uniquely, perfectly disgusting and funny. Justifies 8+ unambiguously.

dialogue.speaker: Chief
dialogue.line: You want a favor from me?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Yes, and it's a big one.

dialogue.speaker: Chief
dialogue.line: Does it involve a calzone?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: No.

dialogue.speaker: Chief
dialogue.line: Then I'm not interested.

jokes.text: The intervention is called. Leslie: 'You have been spending the last 24 hours sipping on joy juice and tripping on Tammy. Well, the people in this room are your methadone.'
jokes.setup: Ron has been Tammy-fied and his friends hold an intervention.
jokes.punchline: Leslie frames Tammy as a drug addiction with the friends as 'methadone' — the clinical language applied to a romantic/demonic situation is perfectly absurd.
jokes.explanation: 'Sipping on joy juice and tripping on Tammy' is strong wordplay — the drug euphemisms map awkwardly but perfectly onto the Tammy situation. 'The people in this room are your methadone' is a great Leslie line: medically accurate-sounding, deeply weird, and delivered with complete sincerity. Quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Oh, wonderful. They got my name right this time.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Jerry Gergich... wait, it says Jerry Gergich-Gergich.

jokes.text: Jerry arrives at the intervention with wedding tumblers from the registry, having misheard 'intervention' as 'reception.'
jokes.setup: The intervention is underway with serious intent.
jokes.punchline: Jerry walks in cheerfully with wedding gifts because he thought it was a reception — perfectly Jerry.
jokes.explanation: Classic Jerry — he misunderstood the situation and arrives inappropriately equipped. The wedding tumblers as gifts for a Tammy wedding are both wrong and horrifyingly appropriate. Good character comedy, solid structure.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I met Tammy at a club. She seemed into me, which was great because I'm very into me.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: We started dating, and everything was perfect until I found out why she actually wanted to be with me.

dialogue.speaker: Tammy
dialogue.line: I only dated you to make your ex-girlfriend jealous.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Wait, which ex?

dialogue.speaker: Tammy
dialogue.line: All of them.

jokes.text: Tom's intervention speech: 'I would like to address the goofy-looking, dirty-kimono-wearing, corn-rowed clown in the room...' ending with 'I hate you like my actual brother, Levondrious, who I hate.'
jokes.setup: Tom takes his turn at the intervention, theoretically trying to help Ron.
jokes.punchline: Tom's speech is ostensibly supportive but is mostly just a series of insults, culminating in 'I hate you like my actual brother, Levondrious, who I hate' — the most specific possible fraternal comparison.
jokes.explanation: Tom's intervention speech inverts the genre: instead of warmth, it's mostly an insult parade delivered as love. The payoff — 'like my actual brother, Levondrious, who I hate' — is great because (a) the name 'Levondrious' is an inspired choice, and (b) the clarification 'who I hate' is a needlessly specific coda that reveals Tom's genuine feelings. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Tammy II
dialogue.line: Why are you hitting yourself? Why are you hitting yourself?

jokes.text: Andy's intervention speech: 'Ron, I do not really understand what is going on right now. But no matter what...' [long beat] 'you must keep going.' Then immediately: 'No. You must stop. I love you, buddy. Follow your dreams.' Leslie: 'Powerful stuff.'
jokes.setup: Andy takes his turn at the intervention.
jokes.punchline: Andy's speech is so confused that he contradicts himself mid-sentence — 'you must keep going' immediately reversed to 'you must stop' — then ends with the useless 'follow your dreams.' Leslie's 'Powerful stuff' is a sarcastic/sincere capper.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional character comedy. Andy's earnest confession of not understanding the situation, followed by a self-contradicting speech that ends with the most generic possible advice, is perfectly Andy Dwyer. The structure of commitment → immediate reversal → generic platitude maps perfectly onto his character's emotional sincerity combined with intellectual vacancy. 'Powerful stuff' from Leslie completes it with dry irony. Justifies 8+ for character integration and the precision of the self-contradiction joke structure.

dialogue.speaker: Tammy
dialogue.line: That was the most pathetic sexual encounter of my life.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I was faking it.

jokes.text: Leslie after Andy's incoherent speech: 'Powerful stuff.'
jokes.setup: Andy has delivered a completely contradictory, confused intervention speech
jokes.punchline: Leslie's sincere assessment of 'Powerful stuff' — she genuinely found it moving — is absurd given what Andy actually said
jokes.explanation: A perfect button to Andy's speech. Leslie's 'Powerful stuff' is simultaneously a reaction beat and a character joke — she's so optimistic and supportive of her friends that she genuinely received Andy's word salad as meaningful. Two words, perfect economy, well-earned laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We could get calzones!

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Yes! Finally, someone who understands me.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: There's a place called 'Calzone's Nightmare' on Fake Street.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: That's... that doesn't sound good.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Or 'The Calzone Zone' on Ben Wyatt Avenue.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Okay, you're just making those up now.

jokes.text: April calls Ann on behalf of Chris, pretending Chris canceled lunch, then April tells Ann that Chris 'doesn't like you' and 'he's not into you sexually.'
jokes.setup: April didn't relay the message correctly earlier; now Ann has arrived to confront Chris.
jokes.punchline: April doubling down — telling Ann that Chris canceled deliberately and 'is not into you sexually' — while Chris is about to walk in and contradict everything.
jokes.explanation: April's sustained campaign against Ann is peak character comedy. 'He's not into you sexually' is a remarkably direct thing to say and delivered with April's flat certainty makes it land hard. The tension of Chris entering to immediately contradict all of this is well-constructed.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I mean, honestly, calzones are just pizza that's angry at you. They're a hot, folded mistake. Every time I eat a calzone, I think about how it's a pizza that couldn't commit to its own shape.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, what are you even talking about?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Just saying, the calzone is an abomination. It's a betrayal of trust. It's bread wrapped around—

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Okay, so we're not getting calzones?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What? No, of course we are. I love calzones. I was just messing with you. Let's go get some right now.

jokes.text: Chris enters: 'April here was very apologetic on the phone. She also sent me flowers. April. Nice touch.'
jokes.setup: April just told Ann that Chris doesn't like her and she did not apologize on the phone.
jokes.punchline: Chris praises April for apologies and flowers she clearly never sent — his excessive positivity makes him blind to April's sabotage.
jokes.explanation: The payoff works because Chris's unshakeable positivity is a character-level joke — he creates the false reality of April's thoughtfulness through sheer optimism. 'Nice touch' is a great button. Good structural callback.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ron, I'm really worried about scarring from the fight.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Scars are good. They make you look tough.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: But what if people think I'm weird?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Only if you're a woman. Women shouldn't have scars. Men should be covered in them.

jokes.text: Ron has made a pre-recorded intervention tape of himself: 'Hello, Ron. It's Ron. If you're watching this, it means that once again you have danced with the devil.'
jokes.setup: The intervention plays a tape Ron made for himself in a lucid moment.
jokes.punchline: 'Hello, Ron. It's Ron' — the self-addressed video is absurd and touching; 'once again' confirms this is a recurring pattern.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best conceits. Ron making a self-intervention tape is perfectly consistent with his character: he is the only authority he trusts, so he has preemptively deputized his future-self to confront his Tammy-addled self. 'Hello, Ron. It's Ron' is a fantastic opening line — funny in itself but also quietly poignant. 'Once again' reveals this is not the first time. The whole conceit is original, character-specific, and structurally elegant. Easily justifies 8+.

jokes.text: Ron's tape: 'Right now, you're probably thinking Tammy's changed. We'll be happy together. But you're only thinking that because she's a monstrous parasite who entered through your privates and lodged herself in your brain.'
jokes.setup: Ron's tape is trying to talk himself out of Tammy.
jokes.punchline: 'a monstrous parasite who entered through your privates and lodged herself in your brain' — Ron's pre-recorded diagnosis of Tammy is horrifyingly specific and anatomically imaginative.
jokes.explanation: 'Entered through your privates and lodged herself in your brain' is a genuinely original metaphor that's both biologically wrong and emotionally accurate. It's maximally gross, maximally specific, and delivered in Ron's clinical internal-memo voice. The phrase 'lodged herself in your brain' via an entry point that doesn't connect to the brain is absurdist biology that somehow makes perfect sense. Justifies 8+ for originality and quotability.

jokes.text: Ron's tape concludes: 'So you have two choices: One, get rid of Tammy, or two, lobotomy and castration. Choose wisely.'
jokes.setup: Ron's tape is presenting its two options.
jokes.punchline: Option two is 'lobotomy and castration' — presented as a reasonable alternative to leaving Tammy, with 'choose wisely' as a perfectly flat closer.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional joke. The binary structure (Tammy OR lobotomy-and-castration) is brilliantly calibrated: it implies that staying with Tammy is as bad as or worse than medical brain-and-reproductive destruction. 'Choose wisely' as an Arthurian grail-quest closer on a penis-and-brain surgery ultimatum is perfectly deadpan. The joke is also a callback to joke #1's micro-penis framing — Tammy's attacks always somehow involve Ron's genitalia. Maximum economy and quotability. Justifies 8+ unambiguously.

jokes.text: Present-day Ron watches his own tape and says: 'You stupid.' Then: 'This is a waste of time. You people have no idea what you're talking about.' Leslie: 'That was YOU on the tape. That was YOU talking.'
jokes.setup: The tape has played and everyone expects it to break through to Ron.
jokes.punchline: Ron dismisses the tape-Ron's advice, prompting Leslie's exasperated 'That was YOU on the tape. That was YOU talking.'
jokes.explanation: The payoff of the tape bit. Ron calling himself 'stupid' and dismissing his own counsel is a perfect escalation — Tammy-Ron is so compromised he's at war with sober-Ron. Leslie's incredulous 'That was YOU talking' articulates the absurdity perfectly. The economy of 'You stupid.' as Ron's self-critique is chef's kiss.

jokes.text: Ron announces: 'Tammy and I are in love, and we're gonna start a family together. In fact, she's ovulating. So if you'll excuse us, we're heading off on our honeymoon.'
jokes.setup: The intervention has failed and Ron is about to leave with Tammy.
jokes.punchline: 'In fact, she's ovulating' — casually disclosed as if it's a relevant scheduling detail.
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'we're in love' to 'she's ovulating' as a parenthetical is the joke — Ron treating ovulation as a scheduling fact that explains his urgency. 'So if you'll excuse us' as a polite farewell in this context is perfectly wrong.

jokes.text: Ron announces the honeymoon plan: '11 days in my cabin in the woods. We bought 10 cases of Gatorade and a 40-pound bag of peanuts for energy.'
jokes.setup: Ron announces their honeymoon destination and supplies.
jokes.punchline: 10 cases of Gatorade and a 40-pound bag of peanuts as the only supplies needed — implying the honeymoon is purely athletic/sexual in nature.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of the supplies is what makes this joke exceptional. '10 cases of Gatorade and a 40-pound bag of peanuts for energy' — with 'for energy' as the devastating explanatory coda — paints a vivid and horrifying picture without saying anything explicit. The quantities are both ridiculous and somehow proportionate. Ron's matter-of-fact delivery of this as a honeymoon itinerary is perfect character work. Highly quotable. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: April delivers a fake urgent memo from 'Bert Macklin, FBI' to get herself transferred back to Parks.
jokes.setup: April doesn't want to work for Chris and wants to return to Parks.
jokes.punchline: The memo is signed 'Love, Bert Macklin, FBI' — Andy's alter-ego FBI persona being used as April's get-out-of-jail card.
jokes.explanation: Bert Macklin is an Andy recurring bit, and its deployment here by April — who uses it as a bureaucratic workaround — is creative. The absurdity of Chris apparently accepting 'Bert Macklin, FBI' as a valid authority source is the payoff. Good character integration across April and Andy's established dynamic.

jokes.text: Chris: 'Dude, I think it sounds like it was Macklin's call.' April's reaction to being let off the hook via a fictional FBI agent.
jokes.setup: April confesses/reveals the fake memo; Chris is trying to process it.
jokes.punchline: Chris, rather than being angry, earnestly suggests that 'Macklin's call' is a valid explanation — his positivity is so encompassing it extends to fictional FBI agents.
jokes.explanation: Chris's inability to confront negativity is so extreme he retroactively validates April's fake memo. The specificity of 'Macklin's call' as an excuse he accepts is absurd and funny. Solid follow-up to the Macklin bit.

jokes.text: Tom's talking head: 'I just wanted to show him what it felt like to have your ex-wife date someone you know. Whatever happened after that is not my fault.'
jokes.setup: Tom is defending his decision to bring Tammy to the party.
jokes.punchline: Tom's logic — 'I just wanted to show him what it felt like' — is both petty and tone-deaf; 'whatever happened after that is not my fault' is the weakest possible disclaimer after causing a marriage.
jokes.explanation: Tom's self-justifying talking head is character-consistent but not particularly elevated. The disclaimer is funny in context (he caused Ron to re-marry a demon) but the construction isn't remarkable.

jokes.text: Ben returns to the chief to ask the real favor. Chief: 'Hey, calzone boy, what's up?' Ben: 'Well, here's hoping that nickname doesn't stick.'
jokes.setup: Ben is back to ask the chief the real favor about harvest festival security.
jokes.punchline: The chief has dubbed Ben 'calzone boy' — the running calzone gag has now generated a demeaning nickname for Ben.
jokes.explanation: The calzone gag has now fully escalated from Leslie's rant to Ben's social failure to an actual nickname. 'Calzone boy' is a perfect endpoint for the running gag. Ben's resigned 'here's hoping that nickname doesn't stick' acknowledges the absurdity perfectly.

jokes.text: Chief: 'You mean, like calzone-sized?' Ben: 'Ah! Sure.'
jokes.setup: Ben says the favor is 'much bigger'; chief uses 'calzone-sized' as the unit of measurement for favor magnitude.
jokes.punchline: Ben has no choice but to agree — 'Ah! Sure' — completing the calzone joke's transformation into a unit of measure.
jokes.explanation: The best beat of the calzone running gag. 'Calzone-sized' as an improvised unit of favor-magnitude is absurdly funny and Ben's reluctant acceptance of the framing is the perfect closing note. Good structural payoff for a well-run gag.

jokes.text: Chief explains why Leslie gets unlimited favors: 'She's the kind of person who uses favors to help other people.' Then: 'Also, my buddy Dave was the crankiest bastard in the department till he started dating Leslie.'
jokes.setup: Ben asks why the chief gives Leslie whatever she asks for.
jokes.punchline: After the warm character endorsement, the chief reveals the real reason: her past relationship with Dave the cop — and Ben's awkward follow-up questions reveal his personal interest.
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the two-beat structure: a genuine compliment about Leslie followed by the real reason (her effect on Dave), and then Ben's increasingly transparent interrogation revealing his feelings for her. 'Are you a pervert?' from the chief is a funny punctuation on Ben's over-interest.

jokes.text: Chief: 'What do you care? You a pervert?' Ben: 'Nope, nope. I'm all good. Um, everything's fine. This is fine.'
jokes.setup: Ben has asked one too many questions about Leslie's dating history.
jokes.punchline: Ben's panicked over-denial ('Nope, nope. I'm all good. Um, everything's fine. This is fine.') is a perfect portrait of someone who has been caught having feelings they're not ready to admit.
jokes.explanation: Ben's cascading reassurances ('I'm all good. Um, everything's fine. This is fine.') are the comedy of self-betrayal. The repetition of 'fine' increases with desperation. Good character work establishing Ben's emerging feelings for Leslie.

jokes.text: April threatens to wear the wedding gift (a terrible sweater or novelty item) to work: 'Don't think I won't do it. I'll wear this to work.'
jokes.setup: The group receives Jerry's wedding tumblers/gift.
jokes.punchline: April threatens to wear whatever was in the gift box as a workplace threat — implying it's unwearable/ridiculous.
jokes.explanation: Mild visual gag — the joke depends on what's in the box (probably a novelty item related to the wedding). April's threat is in character but the joke is incomplete without the visual. Modest score.

jokes.text: They find a new library card in the box. The name on it: 'Tammy Swanson Swanson.'
jokes.setup: They're going through what's presumably Ron's belongings or the wedding gift.
jokes.punchline: 'Tammy Swanson Swanson' — Tammy has taken Ron's last name despite already having it from their first marriage, resulting in the redundant double-Swanson.
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback-based joke. 'Tammy Swanson Swanson' is funny on multiple levels: (1) she eagerly took his name even though she already had it, (2) the redundancy of the double Swanson sounds absurd, and (3) it's discovered on a library card — connecting back to the cold open's library card mischief. Maximum economy (three words, three laughs). Leslie's 'You guys, that's amazing' reaction is the right note. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: Tom tells Ron he brought Tammy as his date because she said 'anything to make Ron miserable' when he asked her — cackled for a full minute before agreeing.
jokes.setup: Tom is coming clean about why Tammy was there.
jokes.punchline: 'She cackled for a full minute and said, and I quote, anything to make Ron miserable.' The villain's honest motivation delivered verbatim.
jokes.explanation: 'She cackled for a full minute' is the key detail — not just laughing, but a sustained villainous cackle. The specificity of 'a full minute' is funny. Tom's dramatic revelation is well-timed within the action sequence.

jokes.text: Tom tries to fight Tammy and fails spectacularly. Tammy: 'Why are you hitting yourself, Glenn? Stop hitting yourself.'
jokes.setup: Tom, trying to protect Ron, attacks Tammy.
jokes.punchline: Tammy — easily overpowering Tom — mocks him with the classic schoolyard 'why are you hitting yourself' while turning his own arm against him, and still calls him 'Glenn.'
jokes.explanation: The 'why are you hitting yourself' is a classic bit elevated by (a) Tammy doing it to an adult man in a police-party brawl, and (b) still calling him Glenn after he's been reminded of his name. The callback to 'Glenn' lands as a secondary punchline. Strong physical comedy inferred from text.

jokes.text: Tammy: 'You're not even a man anymore.' Ron: 'Oh, and by the way, last night, I faked four out of the seven.' Tammy: 'Hmm. So did I.'
jokes.setup: Ron and Tammy are breaking up again. Tammy insults Ron's masculinity.
jokes.punchline: Ron drops the revelation that he faked four of the seven — Tammy immediately matches with 'So did I' — a mutual, simultaneous confession of faking during what was supposed to be the most passionate sex of their lives.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's very best jokes. The structure is perfect: Tammy attacks Ron's masculinity, Ron deploys the nuclear option (he faked), and Tammy's instant 'So did I' transforms what would be a devastating reveal into a mutual humiliation — and somehow a perfect character summary of their entire relationship. The number 'four out of the seven' implies specificity that makes both the faking and the counting funnier. 'Hmm. So did I.' is among the most economical and devastating responses possible. Easily justifies 8+.

jokes.text: Ron tells Tom: 'Let's go, son.' Tom has been called Glenn throughout and physically humiliated. Ron calls him 'son' — paternal dignity restored.
jokes.setup: Ron has just broken free of Tammy's spell and is back to himself.
jokes.punchline: 'Let's go, son' — Ron's first fully Ron-like thing since before Tammy arrived, addressed to Tom who has just been through a brawl on his behalf.
jokes.explanation: 'Son' signals Ron's full recovery — his paternalistic authority is intact. The joke is in the economy of the restoration: two words and Ron is Ron again. The contrast with the kimono-and-cornrow Ron of the past 24 hours makes it satisfying.

jokes.text: Leslie and Ben trade location names for a calzone restaurant: 'over in Idiotville,' 'down on Terrible Idea Avenue,' 'on Beating-a-Dead-Horse Boulevard.'
jokes.setup: Ben makes another calzone reference; Leslie has had enough of the bit.
jokes.punchline: They trade increasingly absurd fake street addresses, culminating in 'beating-a-dead-horse boulevard' — a meta-joke about the calzone gag having gone on too long.
jokes.explanation: A meta callback that doubles as a self-aware acknowledgment that the calzone joke has been milked. 'Beating-a-dead-horse boulevard' is the joke about the joke, and it works because it's mutual — Ben and Leslie are both in on it. The escalating fake geography ('Idiotville' → 'Terrible Idea Avenue' → 'Beating-a-Dead-Horse Boulevard') is well-constructed wordplay.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'Calzones are pointless. They're just pizza that's harder to eat. No one likes them. Good day, sir.' Then immediately: 'I'm just kidding. Let's go.'
jokes.setup: The calzone running gag reaches its final beat — Leslie delivers what sounds like a final, definitive statement.
jokes.punchline: After 'Good day, sir' — a hilariously formal dismissal — Leslie immediately drops the bit: 'I'm just kidding. Let's go.' The puncturing of her own pomposity is the button.
jokes.explanation: The perfect ending to the calzone running gag. 'Good day, sir' is a callback to Ron's earlier 'Good day' and gives Leslie a hilariously pompous curtain line — then she immediately undercuts it with 'I'm just kidding.' The self-deflation is charming and character-specific. Ben's 'Okay. That was funny.' is the right straight-man closer.

jokes.text: Ron explains a scar on his face/head (from the brawl): 'Tom, women like scars. Shows you survived an attack, and they'll assume the attack was from a man.'
jokes.setup: Tom asks if a wound will leave a scar.
jokes.punchline: 'They'll assume the attack was from a man' — Ron's consolation prize is that women won't know Tom was beaten by Tammy.
jokes.explanation: This joke is doing double work: it's both Ron's masculine worldview distilled ('women like scars') and a winking acknowledgment that Tom was beaten by a woman — 'they'll assume the attack was from a man' implies it obviously wasn't. The structure is elegant: comfort → reveal of what actually needs concealing. Strong character integration and economy. Justifies 8 for the economy of information packed into one sentence.

jokes.text: Ron and Tom toast: 'To true love. May we both find it.' Then: 'Nice glasses.' 'Wedding present from Jerry.' 'You're not gonna return them?' 'Nah. Too much hassle.'
jokes.setup: Ron and Tom have a moment of sincere friendship. Tom asks about the glasses.
jokes.punchline: The glasses are from Jerry's (mistaken) wedding gift — and Ron is keeping them out of laziness, not sentiment. 'Too much hassle' as a reason to keep someone's wedding present is perfectly anti-sentimental.
jokes.explanation: A warm closer that callbacks Jerry's mistaken wedding gift. Ron keeping the glasses because returning them is 'too much hassle' is characteristically Ron — pragmatic anti-sentimentality that ends the episode on a quiet, funny note. The callback to Jerry's earlier mistake is a nice structural button.

tmdb_overview: Tom tries to get back at Ron by going out on a date with Ron's ex-wife Tammy, while Leslie tries to protect Ron from falling prey to her charms. Meanwhile, April is assigned to work with Chris.
insight: Ron's vendetta against Tammy II drives 41 jokes at steady 1.81-per-minute pace.
